chunks: Whoever does not find water is to perform tayammum, as God — Mighty and Majestic — said:
The 'sa'eed' (earth) is the elevated place, and the 'tayyib' (wholesome) is that from which water descends,

So when a person wishes to perform tayammum, he strikes his hands on the ground once, then shakes them off and wipes his face with them, then strikes his left hand on the ground and wipes his right hand with it from the elbow to the tips of the fingers, then strikes his right hand on the ground and wipes his left hand with it from the elbow to the tips of the fingers.
It has also been narrated that one wipes his forehead and his eyebrows, and wipes the backs of his hands — and this is how our elders (may God be pleased with them) practiced it.

key_terms.تيمم: Tayammum — dry ablution using clean earth or dust as a substitute for water-based wudu or ghusl
key_terms.صعيد: Sa'eed — elevated ground; here defined as the elevated place from which water flows down
key_terms.طيب: Tayyib — wholesome or pure; here defined as ground from which water descends, i.e. it is not stagnant or polluted
key_terms.مشايخنا: Our elders/masters — the early Shia scholars whose practice validates this secondary narration

ai.seo_question: How is tayammum performed according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This text from Al-Amali of Shaykh al-Saduq provides a detailed jurisprudential ruling on tayammum (dry ablution), the ritual purification substitute used when water is unavailable. The text cites Quran 4:43 and offers a lexical clarification of 'sa'eed' (elevated ground) and 'tayyib' (from which water flows), then prescribes the step-by-step procedure: one strike of both hands, wiping the face, then wiping each arm from elbow to fingertips. A secondary narration adds wiping the forehead, eyebrows, and backs of the hands, endorsed by the early scholars.
